title: Strangler Fig & Migration Patterns
summary: Migrating a monolith to services incrementally, by routing slices of traffic to new code, instead of risking a big-bang rewrite.

slides.markdown:
Deciding to split a [monolith-vs-microservices](monolith-vs-microservices) doesn't mean rewriting it overnight. The **strangler fig pattern** — named after a vine that grows around a host tree and gradually replaces it — migrates one slice of functionality at a time, with the old and new systems running side by side until the old one has nothing left to do.

This topic covers the pattern itself and the practical mechanics of extracting one service without a risky big-bang cutover.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you can't (and shouldn't) rewrite a monolith in one shot
slides.markdown:
A **big-bang rewrite** — freeze feature work, rebuild the whole system from scratch, cut over on one release day — sounds clean but fails predictably. The rewrite team spends months (often years) reimplementing edge cases the original system quietly accumulated over years of production fixes, while the business either keeps changing the old system in parallel (making the rewrite a moving target) or freezes features entirely (losing to competitors in the meantime).

The famous case: Netscape's ground-up rewrite of its browser in the late 1990s took roughly three years, during which Internet Explorer took the market. The rewrite wasn't wrong on technical merits — it was wrong because it bet the whole business on one big cutover with no way to course-correct partway through.

The alternative isn't "don't modernize" — it's modernize in slices you can each validate and roll back independently.

slides.sectionTitle: The strangler fig pattern: routing slices of traffic to the new system
slides.markdown:
The **strangler fig pattern** puts a routing layer (a proxy, an API gateway, or a feature flag) in front of the monolith, then migrates one capability at a time: build the new service for, say, just the "search" feature, then flip the router to send search requests to the new service while everything else still hits the monolith.

Each slice ships independently, gets validated in production with real traffic, and can be rolled back by flipping the router back — no other feature is affected either way. Repeat capability by capability until the router sends nothing to the monolith anymore.

The name fits: like the vine, the new system grows up around the old one, taking over piece by piece, until the original has nothing left to do.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a proxy gradually shifting routes from monolith to new services
slides.markdown:
![Three-panel strangler fig migration: proxy shifting traffic from monolith to services](assets/strangler-fig-migration.svg)

The proxy's routing table is the only thing that changes at each step — no service, old or new, needs to know the migration is happening.

By the final panel, the monolith still exists but handles almost nothing; the migration finishes once the last route is flipped and the monolith is decommissioned entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Extracting a service: data migration and dual-write windows
slides.markdown:
Routing traffic is the easy half; the data is the hard half. When you extract, say, an Inventory capability into its own service, the monolith's database still has the authoritative inventory data other monolith code depends on.

A common approach: during a **dual-write window**, both the monolith and the new Inventory service write to their respective stores for the same operations — often via the new service intercepting writes and also writing back to the old schema (or a CDC pipeline replicating changes both ways) — while you verify the new service's data matches the old system's. Only once you trust the new service's data fully do you cut reads over to it and retire the old table.

Dual-writing is inherently fragile — two writes to two stores are never perfectly atomic — so keep this window as short as possible and monitor for drift actively, rather than treating it as a stable long-term state.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: big-bang rewrite vs incremental strangler migration
slides.markdown:
| | Big-bang rewrite | Strangler fig migration |
|---|---|---|
| Risk per step | All-or-nothing — one cutover, hard to roll back | Small — each slice can be validated and rolled back alone |
| Time to first value | None until the whole rewrite ships | Immediate — first migrated slice ships in production quickly |
| Feature work during migration | Usually frozen or duplicated across old and new | Continues normally on unmigrated parts |
| Total calendar time | Often longer than planned (moving target problem) | Longer in total, but each increment de-risks the next |

**How to decide:** default to the strangler pattern for anything running in production with real users; a big-bang rewrite is only defensible for something with no live traffic yet, or so small a single team can hold the whole thing in their heads through one cutover.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: leaving the strangler proxy in place forever, half-migrated
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We migrated the high-value features already — the remaining monolith code is low-traffic, so it's fine to leave the proxy routing between old and new indefinitely."

**Why it's wrong:** a half-migrated system means engineers permanently pay the cost of understanding two architectures, on-call has to know which system owns which route, and the routing proxy itself becomes a permanent piece of critical infrastructure nobody planned to maintain forever. The "low-traffic" remainder often turns out to still gate something important — a compliance report, an admin tool — that nobody wants to touch, so it never gets prioritized.

**Correct model:** treat the strangler proxy as a temporary migration tool with an explicit end date and owner, and schedule the last, lowest-value slices explicitly — don't let "it's not worth migrating" quietly become "we'll run two architectures forever."

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how long a strangler migration actually takes
slides.subTitle: Estimation
slides.markdown:
A strangler migration's timeline is worth estimating up front, because "gradually" without a number tends to drift into "indefinitely." A mid-sized monolith (say, a few hundred thousand lines, a dozen major feature areas) migrated via strangler fig commonly takes 12-24 months to fully retire, moving roughly one or two feature areas at a time — teams that plan for 3-6 months are almost always surprised by the data-migration and dual-running overhead each slice actually costs.

Concrete example: migrating a "search" feature out first (read-heavy, low write coupling to the rest of the monolith) might take 4-6 weeks; migrating "checkout" later (heavy write coupling to inventory, payments, and shipping) might take 3-4 months for the same team, because the dual-write and reconciliation concerns from the shared-data topic apply in full. Sequencing matters as much as the total timeline — start with the loosely-coupled slices to build confidence in the proxy and migration tooling before attempting the tightly-coupled ones.

The takeaway: put a rough month-count on the whole migration and on each slice, and expect write-heavy, tightly-coupled features to cost several times what read-heavy ones do.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: the migration stalling at 60-70% complete, permanently
slides.markdown:
The strangler proxy is meant to be temporary, but it's common for a migration to stall at 60-70% complete — the easy, loosely-coupled slices get moved quickly, and the hardest, most tightly-coupled 20-30% (often the oldest, most business-critical code, which is exactly why it's tightly coupled) keeps getting deprioritized in favor of new feature work.

The cost of this isn't just "we didn't finish" — it's a permanent tax: the team now maintains *three* systems instead of one (the shrinking monolith, the growing set of new services, and the routing proxy itself), and the proxy's routing rules become their own piece of undocumented, load-bearing legacy that nobody wants to touch. The fix is to treat the last, hardest slice as a scheduled project with its own budget and deadline from the start, not as a "someday" cleanup task competing against roadmap features that always look more urgent.

**Testing:** whether you can name the risk of an indefinitely-stalled migration as a real failure mode, not just a hypothetical worst case — it's the common case, not the rare one.
